children.text: Alburquerque Church is the Santa Monica parish church, about 12km east of Tagbilaran on the coastal road between Baclayon and Loboc. Begun around 1885 in coral stone, it was named an Important Cultural Property in 2013 and received a national historical marker in 2014, and it is quiet enough to explore at an unhurried pace.

The full name of Alburquerque Church (locals shorten the town name to "Albur") is the Santa Monica Parish Church. It belongs to the Diocese of Tagbilaran and stands in the poblacion, right beside Tagbilaran East Road, the coastal road of southwestern Bohol. Wikipedia places the town center about 12km from Tagbilaran, and since it lies on the way from Baclayon to Loboc, you pass it almost automatically on a standard Bohol countryside tour. It is not as famous as the churches of Baclayon or Loboc, but that also means many visitors report almost no one around on weekdays, which makes for a calm visit.

The church began as a visita (mission chapel) of Baclayon. According to Wikipedia, a chapel, convent and school were built in 1842, a larger church followed in 1856, the settlement became a town in 1861, and the parish was formally inaugurated in 1869. During the Spanish colonial era the Augustinian Recollects ran the parish until 1898, after which diocesan clergy took over. The present stone church is said to have been started around 1885 under Fr. Manuel Muro, and its upper walls and bell tower were completed in the 1920s and 1930s. The convent is said to bear the year 1876 above its entrance. Dates differ from source to source, so it is safest to think of it as a church begun in the late 19th century and finished in the early 20th.

The building has a cruciform plan, and the facade shows the typical Bohol arrangement of a choir loft above a row of arches. Inside, thick tree-trunk pillars wrapped in sheet metal line the nave. The original main retablo is gone, but two small neo-Gothic side altars remain at the ends of the transept. The ceiling was painted in 1932 by Ray Francia, and his signature is said to be visible near the choir loft. The square bell tower was added in the early 20th century, and the convent is joined to the church by an arcade.

The magnitude 7.2 Bohol earthquake of October 15, 2013 brought down many churches on the island. Alburquerque Church was partially damaged but relatively lightly, and restoration work that began about three years earlier is said to have helped it avoid major collapse. The National Museum of the Philippines declared it an Important Cultural Property that same year, and in 2014 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) unveiled a historical marker on August 27. This guide relies on a single source, Wikipedia, for the individual designations and dates, so please check the exact wording of the marker on site.
The facade has the Bohol-style choir loft projecting forward above a line of arches. The wide open ground in front lets you take in the whole building from a distance.
A ceiling painted in 1932 covers the nave. Looking for the artist's signature near the choir loft is a small pleasure of its own. When the lighting is dim, the ceiling paintings may be hard to see.
The nave pillars are thick tree trunks wrapped in metal sheets. Some are said to be part of the original structure from around 1880.
The original central retablo is gone, but two small neo-Gothic altars remain at the ends of the transept. They have a plain charm rather than an ornate Baroque look.
The convent is connected to the church by an arcade. The year 1876 is said to be carved above its entrance. Whether visitors can enter depends on the day, so check on the spot.
Two "escuela de niños" (boys' school) buildings from the 1880s are said to stand side by side to the left of the church. With the church, the old walls and rooflines form a single heritage precinct.
Visitors report that, with fewer tour buses than at Baclayon or Loboc, weekdays are quiet. It is a good place to take photos and sit for a moment.
Set out from Tagbilaran. By rental car or day-tour vehicle, drive east along East Road; by public transport, take a jeepney bound for Albur.
Visit Baclayon Church first. Alburquerque was once a visita of Baclayon, so seeing the mother church before the daughter church lets the history flow.

Arrive at Santa Monica Church in Alburquerque. Start with the facade and the wide open ground, then go inside to see the ceiling paintings and side altars. If Mass is in progress, watch quietly from the back.
Walk around the old school buildings to the left of the church and the outside of the convent arcade, taking photos.
Continue toward Loboc for a Loboc River cruise lunch, or go on to Loboc Church.
Travel times vary with road conditions, and I could not confirm official opening hours for the church. Keep the schedule loose and check on the spot.

items.title: Short stop route
items.subtitle: A stopover from a Panglao base

children.text: Leave Panglao by car, pass through Tagbilaran and drive along East Road.
Arrive at Alburquerque Church. Spend about 30 minutes taking a light look at the exterior, interior and convent side.
Continue toward your next stop, the Loboc River or Can-umantad Falls.
There are direct flights from Manila (MNL) to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG). Flight time is around
1 hour 20 minutes
, and airlines and schedules change often, so check before booking.
The airport is on Panglao Island, so you reach Alburquerque by passing through Tagbilaran city and heading east.
Check the latest announcements for flight times and fares from Manila.
Fast ferries run from Cebu City port to Tagbilaran port. Frequency and fares vary by operator and season, so check locally.
After landing at Tagbilaran port, transfer to a jeepney bound for Albur or take a taxi.
Alburquerque lies about
12km
east of Tagbilaran. Visitors report that jeepneys and vans bound for Albur run along Tagbilaran East Road.
One traveler wrote that they came from Baclayon to Albur by jeepney and then waited a long time for the next one. Service may not be frequent, so allow extra time.
The church is in the poblacion beside the road, so you can walk to it from where you get off. It helps to tell the driver "Santa Monica Church."

Lying on the coastal road between Baclayon and Loboc, it is a common stopover added to day countryside tours from Panglao or Tagbilaran. If it is not on the itinerary, ask your driver for a 5–10 minute stop.
The wide open ground in front makes parking fairly easy, but it can get crowded during events.
Alburquerque Church is a place to enjoy the open ground and the exterior, so the dry season is the most comfortable time to go. The whole Bohol countryside tour is easiest between December and May.

The nave is rather dark, so for the ceiling paintings it is better to come after 10:00 when the sun is high. I could not confirm Mass times, so check the diocese or parish announcements. The feast of St. Monica is usually August 27. That date follows the general church calendar, so check locally for the parish's actual events.

It is common to base yourself on Panglao Island or in Tagbilaran and visit Alburquerque as a day trip rather than stay in the town center. There are reports of beach resorts in Alburquerque too, but check whether they are operating at the time. Panglao has lodging and restaurants clustered around Alona Beach, while Tagbilaran has plenty of city hotels and restaurants and convenient transport.

You can have a simple meal at local eateries or street stalls near the church. If you continue toward Loboc, many travelers include the Loboc River cruise buffet lunch. Businesses open and close often, so check before you arrive.
Visiting Baclayon first, then Alburquerque, and finally Loboc makes the history flow naturally, because Alburquerque began as a visita of Baclayon.
By OpenStreetMap, the church is at 9.6113 N, 123.9577 E. Some wiki coordinates point toward Baclayon, so in a map app search for "Santa Monica Church."
The nave is dark, so a fast lens or night mode helps for the ceiling paintings.
Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees. Avoid taking photos and walking around during Mass.
The convent interior may be closed to the public. If you want to enter, ask politely at the office.
Jeepney service can be sparse, so if you go by public transport, allow ample time for the return.
Weekday mornings, when there are few tour groups, are the quietest.
If there is an event on the plaza in front, the entrance gets crowded, so be patient and wait your turn.
This is a working parish church, so stop sightseeing and keep quiet during Mass and prayer times.
I could not confirm official Mass and opening hours, so check the parish announcements before you visit.
With so few tourists around, keep your belongings with you to guard against theft and loss.
It is a heritage building, so do not touch the pillars, walls or altars.
In the rainy season roads can be slippery and flooded, so check the weather.
Dates and designations differ between sources, so check the on-site marker if you plan to cite them.
The mother church of Alburquerque, about
5km
away in a straight line. It is known as the oldest church in Bohol.
About
8km
from Alburquerque in a straight line, it is the classic route of river cruise and lunch.
Bohol's central city, about
12km
from Alburquerque. Its port, hotels and restaurants are clustered here.
A lodging hub with Alona Beach and diving spots. It works well as a base for a day trip.
Bohol's signature inland attraction, a much longer drive from Alburquerque. Linking it into the same day requires an early start.
